karten.v: How can “Response to the rectangular pulse” be derived?
karten.s0: ⁠$t<0$: The shifted $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero only for $\tau\le t<0$, and $s(\tau)$ only for $\tau\ge0$. No overlap, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{g}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$.
s:
⁠$0\le t\le T_0$: Overlap for $0<\tau<t$:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{g(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_0^ta\,\frac1T\,\mathrm{e}^{-(t-\tau)/T}\,\mathrm{d}\tau}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac aT\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/T}\int_0^t\mathrm{e}^{\tau/T}\mathrm{d}\tau}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac aT\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/T}\cdot T\bigl(\mathrm{e}^{t/T}-1\bigr)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{a\bigl(1-\mathrm{e}^{-t/T}\bigr).}$$

⁠$t>T_0$: Overlap only for $0<\tau<T_0$:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{g(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac aT\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/T}\int_0^{T_0}\mathrm{e}^{\tau/T}\mathrm{d}\tau}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{a\bigl(\mathrm{e}^{T_0/T}-1\bigr)\mathrm{e}^{-t/T}.}$$

karten.r: The convolution integral is written in short as the convolution product $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{g(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{s(t)*h(t)}$.
A system with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{h(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\delta(t)}$ passes every signal on unchanged; it is called ideally distortion-free.

karten.z: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{s*h}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\bigl[\operatorname{Re} s*\operatorname{Re} h-\operatorname{Im} s*\operatorname{Im} h\bigr]+\mathrm{j}\bigl[\operatorname{Re} s*\operatorname{Im} h+\operatorname{Im} s*\operatorname{Re} h\bigr].}$$
karten.s0: Substitute $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\tau'}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{t-\tau}$, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\tau}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{t-\tau'}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathrm{d}\tau}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\mathrm{d}\tau'}$.
s:
The limits $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\tau}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mp\infty}$ become $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\tau'}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\pm\infty}$; swapping them cancels the minus sign:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{s*h}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}s(\tau)\,h(t-\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}s(t-\tau')\,h(\tau')\,\mathrm{d}\tau'}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{h*s.}$$

karten.r: $\delta(t)$ is therefore a distribution: an object that is defined only by its effect under an integral, namely by (4.1).
A system with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{h(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\delta(t-t_0)}$ delays every signal by $t_0$; it is called an ideal delay element.
And because the step is the running integral of the impulse, functions with jumps may be differentiated: a jump of height $A$ becomes $A\,\delta$. This is called generalized differentiation.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 7.1 (Properties of the Dirac impulse)”?
karten.r: $$\begin{aligned} &\text{Weight:} && [a\,\delta(t)]*s(t)=a\,s(t),\qquad a_1\delta(t)+a_2\delta(t)=(a_1+a_2)\,\delta(t),\\ &\text{Sifting:} && \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(\tau)\,s(-\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau=s(0),\qquad s(t)\,\delta(t-T)=s(T)\,\delta(t-T),\\ &\text{Area:} && \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}a\,\delta(t)\,\mathrm{d} t=a,\\ &\text{Scaling:} && \delta(bt)=\frac{1}{|b|}\,\delta(t)\quad(b\neq0),\qquad \delta(-t)=\delta(t),\\ &\text{Shifting:} && \delta(t-t_0)*s(t)=s(t-t_0),\\ &\text{Integral:} && \varepsilon(t)=\int_{-\infty}^t\delta(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau,\qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t}\varepsilon(t)=\delta(t). \end{aligned}$$

karten.v: How can “Scaling and the sifting product” be derived?
karten.s0:
⁠Scaling. For $b>0$, with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\vartheta}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{b\tau}$:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\delta(bt)*s(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int\delta(b\tau)\,s(t-\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac1b\int\delta(\vartheta)\,s\Bigl(t-\frac\vartheta b\Bigr)\mathrm{d}\vartheta}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac1b\,s(t).}$$
s: For $b<0$ the substitution reverses the direction of integration, and the result is $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{-\frac1b}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{|b|}}$. So $\delta(bt)$ acts like $\frac1{|b|}\delta(t)$. With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{b}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-1}$ the symmetry $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\delta(-t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\delta(t)}$ follows.

⁠Sifting product. If $s(t)\delta(t)$ is convolved with an arbitrary $g(t)$, the sifting property gives

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{[s(t)\delta(t)]*g(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int s(\tau)\delta(\tau)\,g(t-\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{s(0)\,g(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{[s(0)\delta(t)]*g(t).}$$

Both act identically on every $g$, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{s(t)\delta(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{s(0)\delta(t)}$. Shifting then gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{s(t)\delta(t-T)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{s(T)\delta(t-T)}$.

⁠Integral. $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varepsilon(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\delta(t)*\varepsilon(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int\delta(\tau)\,\varepsilon(t-\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau}$, and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varepsilon(t-\tau)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1}$ exactly for $\tau\le t$.

karten.r: A system with the impulse response $\varepsilon(t)$ forms the running integral of its input; it is called an integrator.
An integrator followed by a differentiator leaves every signal unchanged; the cascade is ideally distortion-free.
A system is called causal if the output does not begin before the input.
A system is called stable (more precisely, BIBO stable, bounded input, bounded output) if it responds to every bounded input $|s(t)|\le A<\infty$ with a bounded output.
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{h(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0\quad\text{for }t<0.}$$
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|h(\tau)|\,\mathrm{d}\tau<\infty.$$

karten.z:
An LTI system is stable if and only if its impulse response is absolutely integrable:

$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|h(\tau)|\,\mathrm{d}\tau<\infty.$$

If $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\int|h|}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\infty}$, choose the least favorable bounded input: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{s(t_1-\tau)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\operatorname{sign}h(\tau)}$, that is, always $\pm1$ with the sign of $h$. Then $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{g(t_1)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int|h(\tau)|\,\mathrm{d}\tau}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\infty}$, although $|s|\le1$.

karten.v: What is the formula “The reference model for this chapter”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{h(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{RC}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/RC}\varepsilon(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm{e}^{-t}\varepsilon(t),\qquad H(p)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{1+pRC}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{p+1},\quad \operatorname{Re} p>-1,}$$

The real part $\sigma$ (in $1/\mathrm s$) is the growth rate: for $\sigma<0$ the building block decays, for $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\sigma}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$ it oscillates with constant amplitude, for $\sigma>0$ it grows.
An absolutely integrable signal ($\int|s(t)|\,\mathrm{d} t<\infty$, so it decays fast enough on both sides) can be built from them.
An absolutely integrable signal ($\int|s(t)|\,\mathrm{d} t<\infty$, so it decays fast enough on both sides) can be built from them. This is the Fourier representation.
The function $\mathcal{F}\{s\}(f)$ is called the spectrum; it gives the weight of the oscillation with frequency $f$.
$S(p)$ itself is a density: weight per frequency interval.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 2.1 (Inversion formula of the Laplace transform)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{s(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm{j}}\int_{\sigma-\mathrm{j}\infty}^{\sigma+\mathrm{j}\infty}S(p)\,\mathrm{e}^{pt}\,\mathrm{d} p }\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S(\sigma+\mathrm{j}2\pi f)\,\mathrm{e}^{(\sigma+\mathrm{j}2\pi f)t}\,\mathrm{d} f.}$$

karten.v: How can “Inversion formula from the Fourier inversion formula” be derived?
karten.s0:
By step 2, $S(\sigma+\mathrm{j}2\pi f)$ is the Fourier spectrum of $s(t)\mathrm{e}^{-\sigma t}$. The Fourier inversion formula gives

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{s(t)\,\mathrm{e}^{-\sigma t}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S(\sigma+\mathrm{j}2\pi f)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{j}2\pi ft}\,\mathrm{d} f.}$$
s:
Multiply by $\mathrm{e}^{\sigma t}$, which does not depend on $f$:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{s(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S(\sigma+\mathrm{j}2\pi f)\,\mathrm{e}^{(\sigma+\mathrm{j}2\pi f)t}\,\mathrm{d} f.}$$

Substitute $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{p}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\sigma+\mathrm{j}2\pi f}$ with $\sigma$ fixed: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathrm{d} p}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm{j}2\pi\,\mathrm{d} f}$, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathrm{d} f}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm{d} p/(2\pi\mathrm{j})}$. The limits $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{f}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mp\infty}$ become $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{p}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\sigma\mp\mathrm{j}\infty}$:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{s(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm{j}}\int_{\sigma-\mathrm{j}\infty}^{\sigma+\mathrm{j}\infty}S(p)\,\mathrm{e}^{pt}\,\mathrm{d} p.}$$

karten.v: What is the formula “The basic transform pairs (used throughout the chapter)”?
karten.r: $$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{e}^{p_0t}\,\varepsilon(t)\quad&\longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{1}{p-p_0},&&\operatorname{Re} p>\operatorname{Re} p_0,\\ -\mathrm{e}^{p_0t}\,\varepsilon(-t)\quad&\longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{1}{p-p_0},&&\operatorname{Re} p<\operatorname{Re} p_0,\\ \delta(t)\quad&\longleftrightarrow\quad1,&&\text{all }p,\\ t\,\varepsilon(t)\quad&\longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{1}{p^2},&&\operatorname{Re} p>0. \end{aligned}$$

karten.v: The region of convergence is the set of all damping rates $\sigma$ for which $s(t)\,\mathrm{e}^{-\sigma t}$ becomes ______.
karten.r: The region of convergence is the set of all damping rates $\sigma$ for which $s(t)\,\mathrm{e}^{-\sigma t}$ becomes absolutely integrable.

karten.v: How can “Basic transform pairs” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{e}^{p_0t}\,\varepsilon(t)\quad&\longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{1}{p-p_0},&&\operatorname{Re} p>\operatorname{Re} p_0,\\ -\mathrm{e}^{p_0t}\,\varepsilon(-t)\quad&\longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{1}{p-p_0},&&\operatorname{Re} p<\operatorname{Re} p_0,\\ \delta(t)\quad&\longleftrightarrow\quad1,&&\text{all }p,\\ t\,\varepsilon(t)\quad&\longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{1}{p^2},&&\operatorname{Re} p>0. \end{aligned}$$
(2.2)(2.3)(2.4)(2.5)
karten.s0: (2.2): $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\int_0^\infty\mathrm{e}^{-(p-p_0)t}\mathrm{d} t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\Bigl[\frac{-\mathrm{e}^{-(p-p_0)t}}{p-p_0}\Bigr]_0^\infty}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{p-p_0}}$. The value at the upper limit vanishes if and only if $\operatorname{Re}(p-p_0)>0$.
s: (2.3): $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{-\int_{-\infty}^0\mathrm{e}^{-(p-p_0)t}\mathrm{d} t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\Bigl[\frac{-\mathrm{e}^{-(p-p_0)t}}{p-p_0}\Bigr]_{-\infty}^0}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{p-p_0}}$. The value for $t\to-\infty$ vanishes if and only if $\operatorname{Re}(p-p_0)<0$.
(2.4): sifting property, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\int\delta(t)\mathrm{e}^{-pt}\mathrm{d} t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm{e}^{0}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1}$.

(2.5): integration by parts, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\int_0^\infty t\,\mathrm{e}^{-pt}\mathrm{d} t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\Bigl[\frac{-t\,\mathrm{e}^{-pt}}{p}\Bigr]_0^\infty+\frac1p\int_0^\infty\mathrm{e}^{-pt}\mathrm{d} t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0+\frac{1}{p^2}}$ for $\operatorname{Re} p>0$.

karten.v: Convolution becomes multiplication because the ______ only multiplies each building block $\mathrm{e}^{pt}$ by the number $H(p)$.
karten.r: Convolution becomes multiplication because the system only multiplies each building block $\mathrm{e}^{pt}$ by the number $H(p)$.

karten.v: How can “Convolution theorem from superposition and eigenfunction” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{g(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{s(t)*h(t)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G(p)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{S(p)\,H(p),}$$
(3.1)

valid for all $p$ that lie in the regions of convergence of both $S$ and $H$.
karten.s0:
Insert the input as the superposition (2.1) into the convolution, using a line $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\operatorname{Re} p}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\sigma}$ that lies in both regions of convergence:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{g(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{s(t)*h(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left[\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm{j}}\int_{\sigma-\mathrm{j}\infty}^{\sigma+\mathrm{j}\infty}S(p)\,\mathrm{e}^{pt}\,\mathrm{d} p\right]*h(t).}$$
s:
Linearity: the convolution may be moved inside the integral, where it acts on each building block separately:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{g(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm{j}}\int_{\sigma-\mathrm{j}\infty}^{\sigma+\mathrm{j}\infty}S(p)\,\bigl[\mathrm{e}^{pt}*h(t)\bigr]\,\mathrm{d} p.}$$

Eigenfunction (1.1): $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathrm{e}^{pt}*h(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{H(p)\,\mathrm{e}^{pt}}$.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{g(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm{j}}\int_{\sigma-\mathrm{j}\infty}^{\sigma+\mathrm{j}\infty}\bigl[S(p)H(p)\bigr]\,\mathrm{e}^{pt}\,\mathrm{d} p.}$$
This is the inversion formula for $g$ with the weight $S(p)H(p)$. Since the weights of a signal are unique, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{G(p)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{S(p)H(p)}$.

karten.r: A conjugate pair of poles $p_r,p_r^*$ together gives a real damped oscillation. This is also the core of stability: a causal building block $\mathrm{e}^{p_r t}\varepsilon(t)$ decays if and only if $\operatorname{Re} p_r<0$.

The pole of the system gives the natural response of the RC circuit, the decay with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{RC}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1}$ s. This holds in general: the output $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{G}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{SH}$ contains the poles of the input and the poles of the system.

Oscillations of different frequencies are therefore called orthogonal.

Multiply (2.1) by $\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{j}2\pi nFt}$, integrate over one period, interchange sum and integral:

karten.r: The average power of the signal is the sum of the powers of the individual harmonics.

A process is called stationary if none of its averages change when all observation times are shifted by the same time $t_0$.
